statement: Kidney injury after MDMA is known from case reports, as described in two narrative reviews, so the figures here are second-hand and the claim cannot say how often it happens; the review of kidney effects writes that, because most of the data come from case reports, 'the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined' (Campbell and Rosner, 2008). As described in that review, most reported episodes of acute kidney injury followed muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after seizures, extreme exertion or overheating, with creatine kinase, a marker of muscle injury, as high as 100,000 U/L or more, sometimes with disordered blood clotting, low blood volume and low blood pressure; the first case, in 1992, took three doses at a rave, and the review says that in the majority of such cases people had been exerting themselves excessively with inadequate hydration and had overheated. In a UK poisons-unit report of 7 deaths with overheating (admission temperatures 40 to 43 degrees Celsius) and 4 further severe cases, summarized in a second narrative review, the most severe cases showed overheating, disordered clotting, muscle breakdown and acute kidney failure together, and plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which the report's authors said did not reflect high doses (Parrott, 2012). Other routes are described in single reports: loss of proximal tubule function in an 18-year-old, vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease in a 30-year-old man 10 days after use and loss of both kidneys from a donor with recent use, blockage at the bladder neck, kidney injury after accelerated high blood pressure, and kidney injury after liver failure; the review says no report of kidney injury after ecstasy has included a kidney biopsy that could show a direct toxic effect, and that causation is hard to attribute when people may have used other substances. In 164 healthy volunteers who took MDMA once or twice in controlled laboratory studies, creatinine (74 against 73 micromoles per litre) and estimated kidney filtration (122 against 125 mL/min) were unchanged on average at screening against about a month after the last dose (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), but these people rested, were healthy, did not overheat or exert themselves, and had no test in the hours or days after the dose, so short-lasting changes are not excluded. The first reported case followed three doses, and none of the reports compares amounts, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk.
plain: Kidney injury after MDMA has been reported in single cases, and nobody can say how often it happens. In most reports it followed muscle breakdown after fits, very hard physical exertion or overheating. A few single cases involved blood-vessel inflammation, a blocked bladder outlet or very high blood pressure. In healthy volunteers who took MDMA once or twice in a laboratory, kidney blood tests were unchanged about a month later, but nobody tested them in the hours and days after the dose, and these people rested and did not overheat. No study compared amounts, so the reports cannot show whether taking more makes it more likely. This comes from reviews of case reports, so it is second-hand.
population: People who developed acute kidney injury after taking ecstasy (MDMA) in published case reports, as described in two narrative reviews; and, as a qualifier, 164 healthy volunteers in controlled laboratory studies who had kidney blood tests before and about a month after one or two doses
exposure: MDMA taken as ecstasy at parties and raves in the reports (first reported case: three doses at a rave); overheating, seizures and extreme exertion with inadequate hydration in the reported cases; in the laboratory, one or two doses of MDMA (study conditions: 75 or 125 mg, at least seven days apart) at rest
comparator: None in the case reports; in the laboratory, the same people's kidney tests at screening, before the study doses
outcome: Acute kidney injury and its reported routes (muscle breakdown, vasculitis, tubule dysfunction, bladder-neck obstruction, malignant hypertension, liver failure); in the laboratory, blood creatinine and estimated kidney filtration
magnitude: Case reports as described in the review (second-hand): no incidence can be given. First reported case 1992, three doses at a rave. Creatine kinase up to 100,000 U/L or more in some cases. Single reports: proximal tubule dysfunction (18-year-old), necrotizing vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease (30-year-old man, 10 days after use), graft loss from a donor with recent use, bladder-neck obstruction, malignant hypertension. UK poisons-unit report as summarized in a second review: 7 deaths with temperatures of 40 to 43 degrees Celsius and 4 further severe cases; plasma MDMA 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l; the most severe cases showed overheating, clotting disorder, muscle breakdown and kidney failure together. Laboratory studies read in full (Vizeli, 164 healthy volunteers, about 29 days after one or two doses): creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (SD 12) micromoles per litre; estimated filtration 122 (SD 22) against 125 (SD 24) mL/min; not significant. No test was made in the hours and days after the dose.

evidence.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs and Table 2 (p. 1854, left and right columns)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: acute kidney injury has been associated with ecstasy, mostly in case reports, so the absolute incidence cannot be determined. The first case report, in 1992, was a person who took three doses of ecstasy at a rave and developed kidney injury attributed to muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after seizures and possibly a direct toxic effect on muscle, with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The review calls non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis the most common scenario and says that in the majority of such cases people had been exerting themselves to excessive levels with inadequate hydration, compounded by impaired temperature regulation and very high temperature; creatine kinase can reach 100,000 U/L or more, and volume depletion and low blood pressure add to the injury from myoglobin. Table 2 lists causes: muscle breakdown (from overheating, extreme exertion, or an unknown direct toxicity), necrotizing vasculitis (rare case reports), bladder-neck obstruction (one case report), malignant hypertension, proximal tubule dysfunction (one case report) and volume depletion.
evidence.quote: the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined

evidence.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, paragraphs on proximal tubule dysfunction, liver failure and vasculitis (p. 1854, right column); paragraph on bladder-neck dysfunction and malignant hypertension (p. 1855, left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: transient glycosuria, phosphaturia and solute diuresis in an 18-year-old (a single report; mechanism unknown, with injury to proximal tubules shown in a rat model); acute liver failure with kidney injury through the hepatorenal syndrome; necrotizing vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease in a 30-year-old man 10 days after use, and graft loss from necrotizing vasculitis in both kidneys of a donor with recent ecstasy use; obstruction from bladder-neck dysfunction; kidney injury after accelerated or malignant hypertension. The review says no case report of kidney injury after ecstasy has had a kidney biopsy that could show a direct toxic effect, and that attributing causation to ecstasy in the vasculitis cases is difficult because the people may have used other substances.

The review concludes that ecstasy use is associated with both kidney injury and low blood sodium, and that most of the episodes of kidney injury are due to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis associated with rhabdomyolysis.

evidence.locator: Section 4 > Clinical hyperthermia and its treatment, 2nd paragraph (p. 5, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review (Henry and colleagues, 1992, UK poisons unit, 1990 and 1991): 7 deaths with overheating, admission temperatures 40 to 43 degrees Celsius; the most severe cases showed overheating, disseminated intravascular coagulation, muscle breakdown and acute renal failure; the authors noted these severe reactions did not reflect high dose levels, with plasma MDMA from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, and other drugs were reported in only one case; four further severe non-fatal cases had temperatures around 40 degrees.

evidence.locator: Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, 1st paragraph (p. 578, right column); Results > Effects of MDMA on kidney and liver function (p. 582, left column); Table 4 (p. 583)
evidence.extracted: Kidney tests in 164 of the 166 healthy volunteers (data missing for two), at screening and at an end-of-study visit on average 29 (SD 22) days after the last of one or two doses of MDMA (the Results text gives 30 +/- 22), 88 (SD 50) days between the visits: creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (SD 12) micromoles per litre and estimated glomerular filtration rate 122 (SD 22) against 125 (SD 24) mL/min, neither significantly different. Liver enzymes were also similar, apart from a small fall in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that laboratory markers of liver and kidney function were assessed only at the end of the study, on average one month after the last dose, which does not exclude short-lasting transient changes; that only healthy, mostly young people were included; and that 166 sessions of MDMA alone (278 with or without a pretreatment) were too small to exclude infrequent or rare adverse events.

risk_of_bias.note: The reviews are narrative and cannot be appraised for bias (high on the cards on the editors' five-domain checklist); the underlying case reports have no comparison group and no kidney biopsies, and causation is hard to attribute.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews agree that the reported injury came mostly with muscle breakdown and overheating; the laboratory kidney tests concern a different situation and are a qualifier.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through two narrative reviews; the primary case reports were not read and have no reference record here.

imprecision.note: No incidence can be derived; the evidence is single reports, and the laboratory estimate rests on one test about a month after the dose.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; case reports are selected by nature, and the claim takes no figure from them.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through narrative reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe (case reports; low) and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3); imprecision is also downgraded because no incidence can be given. Very low. Relation: describes (reported cases, no rate). Status single study: one review was read for the kidney findings, with one line from a second review; the primary reports were not read. Draft: the claim rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3); the laboratory kidney tests are a qualifying anchor, since they concern healthy volunteers at rest and a single test about a month later. The claim does not say that MDMA is or is not toxic to the kidney, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Review-only claim. The primary kidney case reports (Fahal 1992, Woodrow 1995 and others cited by Campbell and Rosner) and the UK poisons-unit report (Henry 1992) have no reference record here and were not read; DOIs not checked. The review's introduction also says the pattern of toxicity is not attributable to overdose and gives an estimated risk of death in people taking it for the first time of 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 (second-hand from one earlier paper); neither is used here because they are not about the kidney.
